issue.title: Potential security concern: Risk of being hacked via malicious code sent through email
issue.body:
There is a potential security concern for users of this repository. If someone sends you an email containing malicious code, and you use that code with this software, you could be at risk of being hacked. Hackers could exploit this by sending code snippets that, when run or opened in uemacs, might compromise your system. 

I recommend users exercise caution when receiving code from untrusted sources and avoid running or opening unsolicited code in uemacs.

issue.title: unwanted trailing blank line on save
issue.body:
Please forgive my impertinence, I'm a MicroEMACS noob - didn't start using it until the fall of 1986.

I'm running 4.0.15 on various Linux distros and my work involves a lot of csv files that are getting awk/grep/sed treatment. When I save a file I've edited with MicroEMACS I often find a single newline appended, even if I went nowhere near the end of the file. If I jump to the end, remove the newline, and leave the cursor at the end of the final line with text then I get the expected result.

This should not be difficult to reproduce, I encounter it several times a day. I do not think it's universal, but I can not yet describe the sort of editing that triggers this event.

issue.title: Bigger filenames should be limited to 127 for now
issue.body:
I did a quick recheck after last commit setting up NFILEN to 256

- **em** crashes when called with filename argument longer than 255 [easy to fix with mystrscpy instead of strcpy]

- as **em** variables size are limited to 127+1, longer filenames will create problems with macroes [ex: $cfname holds the filename of current buffer]

- write-file command can be called with strings up to and longer than 255, so **em** will create files having up to 255 characters, but can't open them either with find-file command or as argument from command line [LOCK ERROR: cannot access lock file - File name too long]

- filenames completion works, a manual display refresh [^L] is necessary to clean up the display.

attached is a simple **em** script I used to generate the files for test: [strip .txt extension]
[tstfnam.cmd.txt](https://github.com/torvalds/uemacs/files/2238479/tstfnam.cmd.txt)

I would suggest to limit NFILEN to 128 for now and fix the strcpy of filename arg issue.

message:
Use the preexisting 'Spell' mode for spell check

According to the readme, that spell mode comes from some odd 'MicroSPELL
1.0' thing, whatever that is. That was back in the '80s, and the only
sign of it in the source code was the MDSPELL mode flag, along with the
parsing of that mode.

But since we do have that mode flag and parsing, just use it to gate the
new spell checking.

Update the emacs.rc file to enable it by default when loading a file,
although I might make it depend on filename etc if I get too annoyed by
the stateless spell checking for source code.

For example, maybe I could enable it by default only for COMMIT_EDITMSG
files. Hmm? With the mode flag, that is trivial to do.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Use pkg-config to find hunspell instead of hardcoding it

Also add -Wall, and fix a compiler warning that showed up as a result.

It's all just slightly less hacky this way.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update README about colorization..

I fixed the most obvious interaction with the ANSI color sequences that
come from git colorizing its output, and this actually works
surprisingly well.  I've been using this _while_ looking at doing the
hunspell thing in uemacs, and I don't actually hate it.

Yes, it ends up bold-facing various random variable names and other
things that aren't proper words, but it's less distracting than I
thought it would be.

I'll still continue to look at uemacs - because catching this while
writing commit messages is better than having "git log" show them later,
but I think I might actually end up using both.

I continue to be surprised that google didn't show any pre-existing
version of this silly tool.  The default output from 'hunspell' (and
'aspell' and friends - I don't want to claim that hunspell would be
particularly bad, quite the reverse) has always struck me as fairly
pointless.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

issue.title: Have you considered using an LLM
issue.body:
https://livebench.ai/#/

You wrote a C program, a Makefile, integrated hunspell, wrapped less, dealt with ANSI escape sequences...

When you could just:
```bash
export GIT_PAGER="your-text | llm --prompt 'highlight typos'"
```

Or even simpler - Claude Opus 4.5 call in a bash alias. Would've taken 30 seconds instead of however long this took.

Local options exist too if you don't want to send kernel commit messages to external APIs - llama.cpp runs fine on CPU.

Just saying. The tool that solves this problem already exists and is smarter than hunspell.

**Title:** Skill issue

**Comment:**

`echo "$msg" | llm "fix typos"` 

🤷

message:
Stop being quite so lazy about line lengths and UTF-8

This deals with line lengths by ignoring the issue and just using a
state machine on raw buffers.

It also deals with UTF-8 content using exactly the same "ignore it" way:
just blithely assume that any non-US-ASCII characters are just letters
in other alphabets.

Because ignorance is bliss, and that makes it do the right thing for
Finnish and Swedish.  And presumably other languages that I don't speak
too.

Of course, if you use use other encodings than UTF-8, you get what you
deserve.  And even with UTF-8, this will get other Unicode things like
half-space characters etc wrong, and just consider it all part of the
word, and call you out on your odd spelling.

You win some, you lose some.  I'm not interested in doing an actual full
Unicode lookup thing.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

issue.title: Add simple TUI for effect and pot control
issue.body:
Closes #11

Simple terminal UI as requested by @torvalds:
> "Some UI for actually turning the virtual 'pots' and picking the effect would probably be interesting. But only something simple."

## What it does
- Select effects (flanger, echo, fm, am, phaser, discont)
- Adjust the 4 virtual pots for each effect
- Process audio and play the result

## Implementation
- Single Python file (~200 lines)
- Uses only curses from standard library
- No external dependencies
- Stays with existing languages (Python already used for visualize.py)

As @ahwelp suggested, this uses Python instead of Rust/Ratatui to avoid adding a new language and heavy dependencies.

## Controls
- Up/Down: Select effect
- Tab: Cycle pots
- Left/Right: Adjust value
- p: Process and play
- r: Reset
- q: Quit

comment.body:
Would you mind looking at expanding this a bit for the new dynamic control functionality I added to the 'convert' binary?

See commit ea71138 ("convert: add somewhat realtime control interface") which talks about changing the pot values at runtime using a file descriptor and the "--control=<fd>" command line switch. I _think_ it should work just fine in your python model.

message:
convert: add somewhat realtime control interface

This is pretty raw and stupid, but I wanted to try changing the
conversion parameters on the fly with a "control file descriptor".

This is currently very limited, and doesn't have an interface for
switching the effect itself at runtime (like I do on the hardware:
long-press the foot-switch for one second), but at least allows for
sending "pot commands" to change the pot values dynamically.

The format is a five-byte ASCII packet of 'pXYY\n', which sets put X to
value YY (X being in the range '0'..'3', and YY being '00'..'99').

Why that format? Because right now the only testing I've done is from
the terminal, doing something like this:

    $ ./convert --control=0 phaser input.raw |
                aplay -c1 -r 48000 -f s32 -B 100

and then you can just type in those commands at the terminal by hand:
the "--control=0" is the magic that says that fd 0 is a control channel.

Very combersome, very stupid, but hey, it works.

Note that I'm back to using 'aplay' for this, because with ffplay the
latency is absolutely horrible.  Something like three seconds of audio
later does any pot command take effect, because ffplay has slurped in a
lot of data into its input buffers.

In contrast, with 'aplay', the effect is basically instantaneous,
particularly with that "-B 100" that keeps the buffering to a very
reasonable 100ms.

If there is a flag for ffplay that makes it not buffer input very much,
I haven't found it (and yes, I tried the obvious ones, but no, I didn't
do any exhaustive search since aplay works fine for me).

It should be very possible to wrap a UI around this, and I should also
add some command to switch the effect at runtime too.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

convert: start parsing arguments more flexibly

In particular, allow default pot values (all at noon), and specifying
input and output files rather than always doing stdin/stdout.

And no, this is still not all that smart, but it is at least a tiny bit
more flexible than it used to be, and the Makefile has been updated
accordingly.

Also, when F_SETPIPE_SZ is available, use it to limit the buffering of
the output if it's a pipe.  That, together with the very limited
buffering by 'make_one_noise()' should make this somewhat real-time if
the target i sreading a pipe and doesn't have huge input buffers.

Put another way: if I add interfaces to modify the pots concurrently,
that hopefully actually takes effect in a timely way.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Refactor visualize.py to use native sample units and improve slider

Dynamically visualize the X axis in different modes, making the raw
sample data the core internal data.  This is similar to how we format
the Y axis.

 - Switch internal logic (view updates, data loading, panning) from
   seconds to sample indices (integers) to match the underlying data
   structure

 - Add 'Samples' vs 'Time' X-axis mode toggle using RadioButtons

 - Update X-axis FuncFormatter to display either integer samples or
   seconds based on selected mode

 - Overhaul slider logic to dynamically switch ranges and formats:
    - In Time mode: Range [0, Duration Seconds], Format '%.3f s'
    - In Samples mode: Range [0, Max Samples], Format '%d'

 - Make the slider be a range slider rather than just showing where the
   current audio window plot starts

This was more antigravity with hand-holding and some manual edits.

Also just update the initial window size to the full audio size (ok,
still limited to one hour), since it's now no longer a performance issue
at least with the test file I have.  Knock wood.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Get rid of too random "helper" functions, tweak pot behavior

Let's avoid the fastpow() helpers as much as possible, because they end
up acting too randomly outside their proper ranges.

I'll have to come up with something better for actual hardware, but for
now, let's pretend that we have a good "pow2()" function, and make it do
the exact thing for simulation for now.

And for frequencies, where we don't want a linear function (because
human hearing response is basically logarithmic) let's use a helper
macro that gives reasonable values: 220Hz to 6.5kHz with the pot
centered giving exactly 1kHz.  A simple cubic function gives a somewhat
reasonable curve.

This all makes the pot values much less random.

Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
